saints.dates: Died in the early seventeenth century; relics uncovered in 1614

summary.text: Juliana is remembered as a married laywoman, mother, widow, and servant of the sick and poor. Her son Kallistrat’s account underlies the church’s memory of a holy life within household responsibilities.

blocks.text: Orphaned young, she lives with relatives who ridicule her devotion. She nurses the sick and sews for the poor. After marriage to Yurii Osoryin she takes charge of the household while continuing prayer and generosity.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of the named modern ecclesiastical life; permission for full reproduction has not been established. Traditional events and miracle narratives remain attributed to that publication.

blocks.text: Begiyan’s essay emphasizes the setting: an ordinary household, relationships, shortages, and the demands of raising children. He presents her care for others as a life sustained through repeated domestic duties, rather than a story requiring withdrawal from married life.

blocks.text: During famine she gives away her last food; during epidemic she cares for the sick. Following the death of two sons she wishes to enter a monastery, but her husband persuades her to remain and raise the children.
blocks.reason: Necessary concise account of the named modern ecclesiastical life; permission for full reproduction has not been established. Traditional events and miracle narratives remain attributed to that publication.

blocks.text: The modern essay discusses the family’s losses, the wish for monastic life, and the husband’s appeal to their remaining responsibilities. It also follows the famine story, when resources run low and charity becomes costly. Juliana’s actions are drawn from her hagiographic life, not offered here as a newly composed rule for readers.

blocks.text: Widowed, she gives her share of the inheritance to the poor. She dies and is buried beside her husband at Saint Lazarus’s church. The life records the discovery of her relics in 1614 and subsequent healings.

blocks.text: Begiyan returns to the spiritual significance of mercy among family and neighbors, using the published life as a lay example. The essay explicitly treats her as a model of righteousness lived in the world. Its interpretation is attributed to its named priest-author; the older life’s extraordinary ascetic details are not turned into personal instructions for the app’s users.

blocks.title: Scripture on widows, family care, and good works — 1 Timothy 5:3–10
blocks.text:
Honour widows that are widows indeed.

But if any widow have children or nephews, let them learn first to shew piety at home, and to requite their parents: for that is good and acceptable before God.

Now she that is a widow indeed, and desolate, trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day.

But she that liveth in pleasure is dead while she liveth.

And these things give in charge, that they may be blameless.

But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.

Let not a widow be taken into the number under threescore years old, having been the wife of one man,

Well reported of for good works; if she have brought up children, if she have lodged strangers, if she have washed the saints’ feet, if she have relieved the afflicted, if she have diligently followed every good work.

death.label: Repose as a widow; no martyrdom by execution in the life
